title: Energy Technologies
summary:
A useful way to read the whole energy system is by what each technology *does for the grid*, not just what it is. Three questions sort almost everything: **Can you control it?** (dispatchable vs variable), **How fast can it change?** (ramp rate), and **Can it store energy, and for how long?** (power vs energy capacity). Keeping those lenses in mind is more valuable to an analyst than memorising any single datasheet.

On the **generation** side, plants trade flexibility against cost. **Baseload** units (nuclear, sometimes large coal) are cheap to run but slow and inflexible. **Mid-merit and peaking** gas plants are the workhorses of flexibility: a **CCGT** (combined-cycle gas turbine) is efficient (~55–60%) and fairly flexible; an **OCGT** (open-cycle) is less efficient but starts fast, so it sets prices at the peak. Hydro — especially reservoir hydro — is the most flexible firm resource there is. Wind and solar are cheap and clean but **variable** and provide little **inertia**, the rotating-mass effect that historically kept grid frequency stable; replacing synchronous plants with inverter-based renewables makes inertia and **grid-forming** capability a growing concern (see gr01).

**Storage** is the system's shock-absorber, and the key idea is that **power and energy are sized separately**. A battery rated '50 MW / 200 MWh' can deliver 50 MW for 4 hours — the **duration** ($E = P\times t$) is what determines what job it can do. **Lithium-ion** dominates short-duration (≈1–4 h) applications: fast, efficient (round-trip ~85–95%), modular, but expensive per kWh for long durations. **Pumped hydro** is ~95% of the world's installed storage — cheap, long-lived, large, but geographically constrained. For **long-duration** storage (days to seasons), the contenders are **green hydrogen** (electrolyse water with surplus power, store the gas, burn it or run a fuel cell later — flexible but low round-trip efficiency, ~30–40%), **flow batteries**, **compressed-air (CAES)** and **thermal** storage. The metric that ties them together is **round-trip efficiency** (energy out ÷ energy in) and, for economics, **LCOS** (levelized cost of storage).

The third pillar is **demand-side flexibility** — instead of building supply to match demand, you flex demand to match supply. **Demand response** pays consumers (industry, EV charging, heat pumps, increasingly data centres) to shift or shed load at key moments. It is often the cheapest 'capacity' on the system and a direct bridge to the grid-and-compute theme: large flexible loads can be an asset, not just a burden.

The synthesis: a decarbonised system pairs cheap variable generation with a portfolio of **flexibility** — fast storage for minutes-to-hours, long-duration storage and flexible gas/hydrogen for the long lulls, and responsive demand to shave the peaks. Matching the *duration* of the problem to the *duration* of the technology is the core design skill.

equations.name: Round-trip efficiency
equations.useWhen: Comparing storage technologies, or finding how much energy is lost in a charge–discharge cycle. Li-ion ~85–95%, pumped hydro ~70–85%, hydrogen ~30–40%.
equations.note: Lower round-trip efficiency means more energy (and cost) wasted per cycle — a key reason hydrogen suits *rare, long* storage rather than daily cycling.

equations.name: Storage energy capacity (duration)
equations.useWhen: Sizing or reading a storage asset. A '50 MW / 200 MWh' battery has duration $t = E/P = 4$ h — it can deliver its rated power for four hours. Power and energy are rated separately.
equations.note: Duration determines the *job*: ~1–4 h (Li-ion) for daily peaks; days–seasons (hydrogen, thermal) for long lulls.

equations.name: Levelized cost of storage (LCOS)
equations.useWhen: Comparing the €/MWh cost of *delivered* stored energy across technologies. Frequent cycling and high round-trip efficiency lower LCOS; rarely-used long-duration storage has high LCOS per MWh.
equations.note: The storage analogue of LCOE. Penalises low round-trip efficiency and few cycles — which is why cheap-per-kWh, rarely-cycled options still struggle economically.

glossary.definition: A plant whose output can be controlled and scheduled on demand (gas, hydro, nuclear-ish). The opposite of variable wind and solar — the property the grid most values for balancing.
Roles by how often a plant runs: baseload (cheap, steady, inflexible — nuclear), mid-merit (CCGT), peaker (runs only at peaks — OCGT). A spectrum of cost vs flexibility.
Gas turbine + steam turbine recovering its exhaust heat; ~55–60% efficient and reasonably flexible. The efficient workhorse of dispatchable fossil generation.
A single gas turbine, no heat recovery; less efficient but starts fast. The classic peaker that often sets the marginal price. (See pm01.)
How fast a plant can change output (MW/min). High ramp rates (OCGT, hydro, batteries) are essential for following variable renewables and demand swings.
Stored rotational kinetic energy in large synchronous generators that resists sudden frequency changes. Falls as inverter-based renewables replace spinning plants — a stability concern.
Grid-following inverters need an existing grid voltage/frequency to sync to; grid-forming ones can *set* it, providing synthetic inertia and enabling very-high-renewable grids.
Energy out ÷ energy in for a storage cycle. Li-ion ~85–95%, pumped hydro ~70–85%, hydrogen ~30–40%. Lower means more loss (and cost) per cycle.
Storage is rated in MW (how fast it can deliver) *and* MWh (how much it holds), sized independently. Their ratio is the duration, $t = E/P$.
How long a store can deliver rated power, $t = E/P$. Short (~1–4 h, Li-ion) handles daily peaks; long (days–seasons, hydrogen/thermal) handles weather lulls.
The dominant short-duration storage: fast, high round-trip efficiency, modular, falling cost — but expensive per kWh for long durations, so best for ~1–4 h jobs.
Pumps water uphill when power is cheap, releases it through turbines when needed. ~95% of installed storage worldwide: cheap, durable, large, but site-constrained.
Green = electrolysed with renewable power (clean); grey = from natural gas (emitting); blue = grey with carbon capture. Colour denotes the production route and emissions.
Splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity. The on-ramp for green hydrogen and a flexible, surplus-soaking load (power-to-X).
Converts hydrogen back to electricity electrochemically (no combustion). The discharge step for hydrogen used as long-duration storage or in transport.
Stores energy in liquid electrolyte tanks; power and energy scale independently, with long life and easy long-duration sizing — promising for multi-hour storage.
Stores energy by compressing air (often in caverns) and expanding it through a turbine later. A long-duration, geology-dependent option.
Stores energy as heat (molten salt, hot water, bricks) for later use or power. Cheap per kWh and well suited to long-duration and industrial heat.
Annualized cost ÷ energy discharged per year (€/MWh) — the storage analogue of LCOE. Rewards high round-trip efficiency and frequent cycling.
Paying consumers to shift or shed load (industry, EV charging, heat pumps, data centres) at key moments. Often the cheapest flexibility and 'capacity' on the system.
Flexing demand to match supply rather than only building supply to match demand. A core, low-cost pillar of a high-renewable system.
The fraction of a store's energy capacity currently filled. Operators dispatch storage to keep SoC ready for the next high-value charge or discharge.
Energy a store loses over time while idle. Low for pumped hydro, higher for some batteries — a key drawback for long-duration storage.
The ability to restart generation without an external grid supply, to bring a collapsed system back up. Traditionally from hydro/diesel; now also batteries.
Using (surplus) electricity to make other energy carriers or feedstocks — hydrogen, ammonia, synthetic fuels, heat. Links the power system to industry and long-duration storage.
Factory-built, smaller nuclear units aiming for lower cost and siting flexibility, including potential co-location with large loads like data centres. (See gr01.)

tips: **Sort every technology by three questions:** dispatchable or variable? how fast does it ramp? can it store, and for how long? That framing beats memorising datasheets.
**Power (MW) and energy (MWh) are sized separately.** A storage asset's job is set by its *duration* $t = E/P$ — 4 h of Li-ion solves daily peaks, not a week-long wind lull.
**Match duration to the problem.** Short, frequent gaps → batteries; long, rare lulls → hydrogen/thermal. Round-trip efficiency matters less for rarely-used long-duration storage.
**Low round-trip efficiency suits rare use.** Hydrogen's ~30–40% would be ruinous for daily cycling but acceptable for seasonal storage that runs a few times a year.
**Inertia is the hidden service.** As synchronous plants retire, frequency stability and grid-forming inverters become real constraints — not just 'how many MWh of renewables'.
**Demand is a resource, not just a load.** Flexible demand (heat pumps, EVs, data centres) is often the cheapest balancing tool — the bridge to the grid-and-compute thesis in gr01.
